sections.content:
Before midterm focuses a lot in 3D geometry, namely curves, lines and planes, with a little bit of partial differentiation. In some sense it's like the vector part in DSE M2 given the emphasis on geometry (comparing with 2111 which is more algebraic). After midterm it's all differentiation and integration, but it's much simpler that most of it is just applying formulas.

For physics and engineering students probably the geometry is useful, but maybe a bit too much for econ, CS or IEDA students who are using multivariable calculus for optimization most of the time.

One recommendation is that instead of the common physical examples like work done, you may ask AI to give some other simple examples in fields (no pun intended) you're familiar with (e.g. econ -> consumer surplus).

He doesn't have lecture notes in pdf but instead he uses Geogebra, which might be helpful for some but I don't find it particularly interesting. Most of the time I just read the notes from MATH2023. The tutorial notes shared by MTR553891 are also pretty nice, which I printed out in the open book exams.

He makes clear, handwritten notes that explain the content thoroughly, and it is very legible. His classes are straightforward, and though it may not be the most interesting class, he goes out of his way to find examples that apply to the majors of students in his class. Your standard Calc 3 content, but not as rigorous than its Math2023 counterpart. Please refer to other comments for details, there is no syllabus change. Green's theorem/ Stokes theorem is not included.

Textbook: Stewart's Calculus (Early transcendentals)

Stewart's writing in the multivariable part of the textbook is utterly disgusting. Stewart's book sometimes offer an overtly simplistic view in his examples. Instead,I use the book Vector Calculus by Susan Colley (4th edition). The textbook is free online (along with solutions). This book is definitely made in mind for math majors, but it is good enough for any engineering student. Unlike Stewart, the example questions actually helps as she doesn't skim out on the details. You definitely do not need to cover all of Susan Colley's book, but hey, it's a real good reading experience , even for someone who's math allergic.

sections.teaching:
QIAN, Tiezheng's teaching straightforward, and provides concise, practical explanations. My friends liked his teaching, and they did quite well. I think the teaching was the best I have seen thus far in MATH. However, it didn't have a drastic impact on me. If you prefer a more comprehensive approach, I suggest you use a textbook. Personally, I used the Thomas' Calculus by George B. Thomas, Jr. I liked it because I found it quite instructive. It also has great practice problems, and its layout matches the syllabus of the course.

The tutorial is alright. The tutor was quiet but was willing to respond to questions in class. I have seen way worse.

The past paper is a ruse, especially the midterm. Please do not be convinced that the midterm will actually appear like that. Recollect your experience in MATH 1013 and MATH 1014. There is no free warm meal in MATH.

sections.teaching:
I first enrolled in Professor Wang's class, and her first lecture was terrible. I have not seen any lectures like hers. I suppose it was her first time teaching, and she seemed extremely nervous and could not even say things right. She literally read the slides and followed the materials without any explanation. I quickly switched to Professor Qian's class.

Professor Qian was a fairly good professor, he is quite humourous and likes to joke around with students. I don't think his no-phone policy was too bad, but it ultimately comes down to personal preference. He explains the materials pretty well, and he loves to draw graphs and diagrams as he's teaching, so we can get a good visualization. I ultimately stopped attending his lessons because I couldn't catch up with what he was teaching and his attitude towards students with questions was not up to my tastes.

I switched to watching Professor Leonard's videos thanks to the comments here and he is literally a blessing to us students. I can feel his passion for teaching and how he loves his students, which I think is an essential quality of a good teacher. He also explains his materials really well, though a bit too lengthy sometimes, but you can turn it up to 2x speed and it's ok.

I eventually watched all of Professor Leonard's videos because it's more than the scope of this course and because he links up concepts really well. So even for slower students like me it's easy to understand. Please save his playlist and watch his videos, he's going to be teaching better than any professor from this course. I got around 30 in the midterm because I couldn't understand my professor, and I got 84 in the finals thanks to Professor Leonard and got an A.

Here's a link to his playlist:
https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDesaqWTN6ESk16YRmzuJ8f6-rnuy0Ry7&si=OLvwOWfFbpNkQAq3

sections.teaching:
I don't really like WU Lixin teaching style. Pretty boring I would say. At least not as bad as Xiong Maosheng. But my first impression from him is quite poor. He casually shows some matlab code and explains it for 30-40 mins. I don't think it is necessary to do that and I had a feeling he will do same for the next few lectures so I skipped pretty much all of his lectures. Then I realized that his speed on teaching is really fast. Just by looking at the syllabus for the mid term (Up to 14.1 Planes and Curves) vs the current topic he is teaching (15.6 Multiple Integrals). idk how he taught that quick but I was able to catch quite quickly by myself. Also, the lecture slides are just from the book publisher. So no hand written stuff inside. There is other notes from L1 which is wayyy better than WU's.

The TA I had this time is pretty meh as well. The tutorials are just reminder for the topics and nothing more is done after that. No exercises, no support at all, literally hear nothing from them. This is kinda sad. The TA also don't share the slides to us on Canvas as well.

For me, I just purchase the textbook. Really thick book but really useful since you have a lot of practice to do and you can always get a full understanding from the topics, questions. You don't really need to buy it but you can get one in the library they are quite similar anyway so go get one for yourselves if you don't have any exercises to strengthen yourself.

- Vector-valued Functions (limits + easy calculus)
- Motion in Space (physics, abstract)
- Length and Arclength parametrization of Curves (just rmb formula)
- Curvatures of Curves (just rmb formula)

- Partial Derivatives (very easy)
- Chain Rule, Implicit Differetiation (easy)

- Max/Min Problem (need practice)
- Lagrange Multiplier [NEW!!] (need practice)

(all are good tools but need imagination, practice makes perfect)
- Double Integrals in Rectangular Coordinates
- Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates
- Triple Integrals in Rectangular Coordinates
- Triple Integrals in Cylindrical Coordinates
- Triple Integrals in Spherical Coordinates [Optional]

Chapter 4: Vector Fields
(mainly focus on 2D, abstract but amazing)
- Line Integrals of Vector Fields

I don't attend any lectures because I watched the recordings provided by Prof. Lu but I think watching Youtube Prof. Leonard is much more useful for this course.

Prof. Lu is willing to answer questions through email. And he is also helpful in giving some supplemental resources.

Copied from his email:
Make sure you can understand all the examples in the notes. They are important since some of the questions in our exams will be modified from the examples. For more materials, you can read our textbook Stewart's Calculus. For example, parametric equations and polar coordinates are covered by Sections 10.1 to 10.4. The contents in our last two lectures are covered by Sections 12.1 to 12.5. You can also try to do the exercises in this book. But this book lacks answers to some of its exercises. (It shows only the answers to odd-numbered questions.)

Demidovich's Problems in Mathematical Analysis will be another useful exercise book. It is a famous problems set that contains more than 3000 problems with hints or answers. Since the order of the chapters in this book is different from ours, you could make good use of Ctrl+F to find the topics you are interested in. I have attached a djvu version with this email. To open this file, you need a djvu reader. The reader for djvu files can be found in "djvu" official sites and be downloaded free. By the djvu reader, you can ask it to list all the findings matching your key words. For example, if you want to practice with some parametric curves, you may search "paramet" and then press "All". Then you can check the findings one by one in the window that pops up on your left.

sections.content:
Overall the content is interesting, and easier than Math1014.

The most annoying part is memorising all the formulas like
arclength, unit tangent, unit normal, curvature >_>. the list kinda just goes on.

if you can do derivatives, you can do partial derivatives. you legit just treat all but one of the variables like it is a constant, and then you take the derivative.

double integration is more of a nuisance. If you know how to do the set-up, you can do anything the teacher throws at you. please get comfortable with polar regions because they are a life saver. You don't have to worry about spherical coordinates in this course.

triple integration is just double integration except its annoying as frick. if you ever want to change the order of integration(which in double integration, you have to draw the 2d region), ur gonna have to draw out a nice 3d surface, or a ton of 2d regions and use ur brain and figure out what to do from there. you better pray you don't have to do triple integral bound changes on the exam :) ALSO, there is a way to avoid trig sub that isn't taught in class. Its called the jacobian, please for the love of God learn jacobian substitution on your own.

Vector fields: we basically skipped everything useful this semester >_< we can do line integrals over vector fields and conservative vector fields. But we never learnt green's, stoke's or divergence theorem, which are really important for engineering courses.

looking back, i regret not doing 2023. If you want a complete package of multivariable calc, do math2023.

Course content includes:
*General introduction of 3D space
*Vectors and vector operation
*Lines and planes in 3D space
*Vector functions
*Multivariable functions

**Maximum/minimum values of multivariable functions

While mentioned in other previous reviews, the divergence theorem and Stoke’s theorem were not taught, though Professor Ho did encourage us to self-learn them if we want to have a more solid understanding on multivarible calculus.

Previous M2 experience may help with understanding vectors, but after the topic of 3D lines and planes, you can no longer rely on your previous knowledge. These knowledge will be useful when you learn further in your major (eg. MECH2210 for MECH/AE students).
sections.teaching:
In general, Professor Ho teaches in a slow, steady, yet easy-to-understand way. As a local professor, his accent is understandable, and he also maintain fairly vibrant interactions in lectures. While previously reported that the course's notes must be taken from his lectures, all lecture notes are available on Canvas this semester.

One of his specialty is using paper and coloured pens instead of using pre-made PowerPoint during teaching, which helps with understanding the 3D coordinate system and drawing. Examples discussed in lectures are also dissected in details and guided step-to-step, with more emphasis on application than proof, though you can listen to his explanation should you know learn deeper.

I'll consider him similar to Merkel: not exceptionally shiny or attractive in teaching, but with sufficient experience, he also teaches well.

Speaking of the TA, Ho Ming Leung is as unremarkable as other MATH TAs I've experienced before: Simply finding today tutorial's notes, and do questions in front of us, in which I mostly uses the time to do questions by myself. Another criticism is that he used unproportionate time to explain some easy contents, like the answer of one presentation question, while simply don't mention about other contents (like how to solve midterm questions) we'll concern more.

P.S. As mentioned by other students, Professor Ho is known for repeatedly sending email notifications to us (probably on average, 5-6 emails per notification). While regular cleanup can be a solution, your email system organizes forwarded/replied emails into a single one, so you may also opt to delete all notifications when he don't repeat them and you consider they're useless.

sections.grading:
I see that many students have posted reviews blaming Prof QIAN fore his grading scheme arrangements especially after what happened in the midterm. I actually have a different point of view, for those who hate and suffered from this kind of arrangement, please accept my sincere sympathy. But I will not blame Prof QIAN for this eventual arrangement as personnaly I think this is already the best arrangement after what happened in the midterm.

1. The Prof doesn't hope for the technical issues during the midterm either. he tried his best to arrange a midterm under such a difficult period, and he was willing to hear from students' different advice after what happened, at least we have nothing to blame for his attitude.
2. Some may think that voiding the midterm and "taking it as a good exercise" is irresponsible. But the fact is that, the influence of the technical issue in the midterm is high enough to affect a lot more than the students who didn't have their answers recorded. Firstly, during the last 15 min of the exam , the whole proctoring zoom meeting is filled with noise about students and professors discussing about the technincal issues, for an exam that requires you to finish 30 questions in 1 hour, I don't need to tell you how tight is the time and how annoying it is to hear all that noise in the last 15 mins of the exam. So the noise effect is one thing. What's more is that many students who have score recorded didn't get their real score recorded. Like if he/she submitted once at 20 min, then he/she didn't preview and submitted again at last, the second time the answers will not be recorded and he/she can only receive points for the first 20min answering period. So even with a "recorded score", as 80% of the students did, the recorded score may not be the real deserved score.
3. Many blamed that all the efforts studying for the midterm become a waste due to the arrangements. But isn't it our duty as a student to understand the contents of courses as best as we can? the studying for the midterm will be helpful for the final as well and certainly helful for understanding the whole course.

Now to the eventual grading scheme. 30%HW+70%Final, this is already better than math1014 which has 75%final. So I am satisfied enough with his arrangements. He couldn't have done much better. But I do hope Prof Qian can learn a lesson from the midterm techinal issues and make this a even better course in the future. For those who took advantage from this arrangement change, Congratulations! For those who suffered loss, please accept my sincere sympathy but let's not blame the prof too much of this. He already tried to make it as fair as possible.

sections.content:
MATH 2011 is an easier version of its sibling course, MATH 2023.

This course targets at students from engineering school and has more emphasis on the applications of multi-variable calculus in engineering topics. The content covered will be useful for further studies in fluid mechanics, electronics etc.

Topics included:
1. Vectors, dot product, cross product and its applications
2. Lines, Planes and vector applications (** find shortest distance)
3. Cylinders and Surfaces
4. Vector-valued functions (limit, derivatives, integrals, tangent line, arc length and re-parametrizaton, sketching)

5. Function of two variables, domains, range, level curve, continuity, limit (use two path test to proof non-existence of limit)
6. Coordinate systems conversion
7. Partial Differentiation, chain rule (draw dependence chart), implicit differentiation
8. Gradient vectors, directional derivatives and its applications (normal line, tangent plane, equation of tangent line etc)
9. Linear approxiamtion
____________________________________

10. Extreme value and its applications

11. Double integration under general, rectangular region (Fubini's Theorem)
12. Double integration under polar coordinate system
13. Surface Area and its aoplications
14. Triple Integrals under rectangular and cylindrical coordinate system

15. Line Integrals under vector field (find work done/fluid flow)
16. Vector fields
17. Conservative vector field (find potential function, Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals, Path independence)
18. Divergence and Curl
19. Green's Theorem
20. Surface Area and Surface Integrals
21. Flux and Divergence Theorem

(Stoke's Theorem is omitted this semester)
sections.teaching:
I have no doubt to say that HHM saves my life and brings me back to heaven this semester since I didn't perform well in Year 1 Math courses.
He really devotes a lot in teaching and cares about the delivery of content. See below.

1. Lecture Notes
Printed colorful lecture notes are distributed in every lecture. The notes included most of the key concepts with detailed explanation, proofs and graphics. Dr Ho would explain the concepts in detail with his amazing great handwriting and sketching, as well as in-class demonstrations using different tools to help visualize the effects of concepts. Not only concepts would be delivered, he also spends time on computing significant examples, explaining in a way that you should have no problem to understand well. The content are well delivered and organized in general. I never find his lecture boring since he is really serious in teaching and the logic is easy to follow since he acts like a robot with his distinctive tone.

Some examples of Dr. Ho lecture presentation
Things to do: When we compute .....
Is that true for ....? Please raise up your hand? one, two, three... thank you! thank you! The answer is NONE OF THEM!
Draw smiling faces :) :) :)  then he smiles with his creepy face :)
please fasten your seatbelt
This is the first, second, third reminder ...... (He is an email sadist)

2. Additional Examples on Canvas
Dr. Ho won't cover the additional examples in class but I still recommend you to print them out and understand the materials. These help you to get a concrete and integrated understanding between topics.

Tutorials:
My tutor is Tommy Cheng. Although he speaks Konglish and broken English really well, he is able to demonstrate extra examples which are not covered in lectures. His tutorials are basically using the notes prepared by Einstein and the whole tutorial is simply examples drilling.

sections.teaching:
Prof. Qian's content for this course is comparatively easier than Dr Ho Hon Ming's after reading both of their notes so I recommend taking this course in a semester with Prof. Qian. (unless you actually want to learn more, then take Dr Ho's class). Also, we ran out of time to teach Green's theorem which made the course easier as well. I think he teaches quite well, provides some simple and good examples and the class is not extremely boring. The first few lectures were pretty simple and rather basic content but get exponentially harder later on especially topic 4 and 5. He will do some pretty difficult proofs in class but do not worry about those as this course is purely computational, so just understand the calculations and how to get to the answer (the process is important). Lecture video is also provided so there is no need to really attend lectures.

For tutorials, just a very short tutorial exercise, teaching for tutorials were not great but it is ok. A lot fewer exercises to practice from than teaching staff from MSC. Could skip it as TA's notes are online and he just goes through the exercise. Just use them for practice for exams.

The midterm was more straightforward than the final, but I think both of the exams were not extremely difficult, just have to make sure you really understand the content before which is the most difficult part, applying the content to the questions once you understand it is relatively simple.

Exam grades are pretty varied with quite a few getting full marks and quite a few also getting pretty low marks, so either you understand the content or not.

sections.workload:
12 homework on webwork: the first few were quite easy but gets harder later on. They are actually pretty good practice for exams. If you are a deadline fighter, a lot of the homework later on (especially the integrals) could just be done online as long as you plug in the correct integral and its limits (saves time for computation).

To do well in this course, also make sure you understand at general one-variable calculus and are able to do questions from there well e.g. from 1000 math courses or else you might struggle with the integrals computationally. But I think overall the questions in exams computationally (not conceptionally) should be easier than in math 1000s.

For exams, I suggest just use tutorials for practice. It is pretty sufficient for Prof. Qian's exams which are relatively easy as its nearly all computational questions (one question in final about different surfaces). Understanding the concept is most important as it gets pretty abstract later on, so make sure you read through the lecture notes.

You can say there are a lot of new concepts in this course:
- Equations of lines and planes in space
- Space curves
- Differential Calculus of Multivariable Functions (Limit, continuity, partial derivatives, chain rule, tangent plane, max and min)
- Multiple Integrals (Double and Triple Integrals)
- Vector Calculus (Line integral, surface integral, flux, divergence, potential, and the three fundamental theorems that link between concepts of multiple integrals and vector calculus)
(Note: Stokes' Theorem was not tested)

It is like cramming the whole 1013 and 1014 into one course, and adding more new things at the same time.

However, you can also say many of them are old things that are just some extended versions to 2D plane or 3D space of the things that are already taught in 1013 and 1014.

So, if you have to take this course, you are encouraged to do better in 1013 and 1014, which helps you get a better picture between the many different concepts introduced here. This possibly makes the course significantly easier.

Or else, you may well need to re-visit the concepts in 1013 and 1014 frequently, and simultaneously learning many "new" things. That would be no good, right?

The content is a bit harder than what we have learned in MATH1014 and requires integration techniques and similar concepts in MATH1014. The contents after midterm are much harder than what I learned before the midterm.

2. Vector-valued functions, Motion in space, Length of curves
3. Functions of several variables, level curves, limits and continuity of functions of several variables
4. Conversion between cylindrical, rectangular and spherical coordinate systems, partial derivatives, Chain rules.
5. Gradient vectors, Tangent planes  
Tangent planes on the aspect of approximation, Extreme values

6. Double integration on rectangular regions, double integration on general regions, polar coordinate system
7. Double integrals in polar coordinate, surface area, triple integrals in rectangular coordinate system.
8. Triple integrals in cylindrical coordinate system, line integrals, vector fields and line integrals in vector fields
9. Flux of a vector field, path independence, potential functions and conservative vector fields and Green’s theorem in the plane
10. Surface integrals, flux of a vector field across a surface
11. Divergence theorem

sections.content:
This course splits into two main topics: Vectors and Calculus.

For vectors, the course includes basic vectors calculation like addition, subtraction, dot product and cross product of vectors. It also teaches how to find planes and lines equations by vectors. And gradient vectors and directional derivatives is included too.

For calculus, partial derivatives, double and triple integrals, line integral, surface integrals, Green's Theorem and Divergence Theorem. Maybe includes Stroke's Theorem but the lecturer didn't have enough time to finish it so it didn't appear in final exam.

For me, the most difficult topics are using vectors to find distances between two lines/planes and surface integrals. But overall the calculus part is easier than the vector part.
